card.title: First and Last Position of a Value

a1.cap: nums is sorted ascending (values may repeat). Return [first, last], the first and last index of target, or [-1, -1] if it does not appear. Use O(log n).
a1.say: nums is sorted ascending (values may repeat). Return first, last, the first and last index of target, or -1, -1 if it does not appear. Use O of log n.

lines: nums is sorted ascending (values may repeat). Return [first, last], the first and last index of target, or [-1, -1] if it does not appear. Use O(log n).

a1.cap: For example, with nums = [5,7,7,8,8,10], target = 8, the answer is [3,4].
a1.say: For example, with nums equals 5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10, target equals 8, the answer is 3, 4.

a1.cap: The first position of the target is the lower bound of target. The last position is one before the lower bound of target + 1.
a1.say: The first position of the target is the lower bound of target. The last position is one before the lower bound of target plus 1.

a1.cap: So the same small binary search answers both questions.
Let's walk through it with nums = [5,7,7,8,8,10], target = 8.
a1.say: Let's walk through it with nums equals 5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10, target equals 8.

a1.cap: The first index with a value of at least 8 is 3.
The last copy sits just before that: index 4.
The first index with a value of at least 9 is 5.
Time complexity is O(log n) and extra space is O(1).
a1.say: Time complexity is O of log n and extra space is O of one.

a1.cap: That's the Two Lower-Bound Searches approach. Now try writing it yourself, in Java or Python!
